title: Counting the Omer
hook: Jews count seven weeks of days from Passover to Shavuot, some giving each day a quality

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Musar: character work, one trait at a time. Your line was one trait.

During Passover, in Jewish homes and synagogues, someone says a blessing in the evening and then one short sentence: today is one day of the Omer. The next evening: today is two days of the Omer. Then three. Then four. A number said out loud, and nothing else to do. No meal attached to it, no special clothes. Just the number, growing, all the way to the festival of Shavuot. And yet it has its own blessing, its own rules, and an old question about what happens if you forget.
screen: `TODAY IS ONE DAY OF THE OMER.` → `NIGHT AFTER NIGHT, A NUMBER.` → `ALL THE WAY TO SHAVUOT.`

segments.voice: The count comes straight from the Torah. Leviticus says, in the King James wording: "And ye shall count unto you from the morrow after the sabbath, from the day that ye brought the sheaf of the wave offering; seven sabbaths shall be complete." That sheaf is the omer, an offering of new grain from the harvest. Seven weeks of days, counted one by one, then a festival: Shavuot, the Feast of Weeks. Passover remembers leaving Egypt. Shavuot, tradition says, remembers the giving of the Torah at Sinai. So the count walks a road, from being set free to being given something to live by. And it's a count up, not a countdown. A countdown treats the days in between as a waiting room. A count up adds each day to the total, so every one of them is kept. Over time a second layer grew. Some Jews, following the kabbalists, give each of the seven weeks a quality, starting with chesed, loving-kindness, and each day within the week a shade of those qualities: loving-kindness within loving-kindness, strength within loving-kindness. Then the rabbis add a very human question: what about someone who forgets to count for a whole day? One well-known ruling says keep counting, but without the blessing. A missed night doesn't send anyone back to the start.
screen: `THE SHEAF, AND SEVEN WEEKS.` · `FROM FREEDOM TO SINAI.` · `A COUNT UP, NOT A COUNTDOWN.` · `A QUALITY FOR EACH DAY.` · then, large: `SEVEN SABBATHS SHALL BE COMPLETE.`

segments.voice: Take the quality the count begins with, loving-kindness, and look for it in your last day: where it came easily, and where it stalled or went missing, without grading yourself. Then say quietly inside, the way a counter would: today is one. If you pray, you can hold that day before God; if you don't, just hold it in your attention, breath by breath.
Counting the Omer. Seven weeks of days, counted aloud one by one from Passover to Shavuot, and for some, a quality for every day. Today's word.
Your line: count the days. The count is too important to drop over one missed night. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jews who keep the count say a blessing each evening from the second night of Passover and then state the day's number of the Omer until Shavuot; some also reflect on a kabbalistic quality assigned to that day.

chat.says: If you forget to count the Omer one night, do you have to start over?
options: No; one well-known ruling says keep counting, just without the blessing.
Yes; the seven weeks must be complete, so you begin again at day one.
Only in the first week; after that, missed nights don't matter at all.
chat.meaning: One well-known ruling says to keep counting without the blessing. The count is too important to drop, and a missed night doesn't reset it.

notes: Confirm KJV wording of Leviticus 23:15 as quoted.

The omer is described as 'an offering of new grain from the harvest' (Lev 23:10: 'a sheaf of the firstfruits of your harvest'); the rabbinic identification as barley is not stated in the voice. The original-game note calls omer 'a sheaf, and a measure of grain'; confirm.
Shavuot as the remembrance of the giving of the Torah is framed as 'tradition says' (it is not stated in the Torah). Confirm.

The kabbalistic scheme (seven weeks = seven lower sefirot, starting with chesed; each day a sefirah within a sefirah) is attributed to 'some Jews, following the kabbalists'. Confirm 'strength within loving-kindness' (gevurah she-bechesed) as day two.
Missed-day ruling: Shulchan Aruch OC 489:8 (one who missed a whole day continues counting without a blessing); presented as 'one well-known ruling' since opinions differ. Confirm.
howItsDone says the count begins on the second night of Passover (rabbinic reading of 'the morrow after the sabbath'); this is in howItsDone only, not the voice. Confirm.
Index hook says forty-nine days; the script says 'seven weeks of days' following the cited text ('seven sabbaths shall be complete').
Practice and carry: homework (begin a count of your own this week) removed; 'the count is too important to drop' moved from the teach to the carry so it is said once.
